Nearby context: Rashi’s nearby comment on 32:2;

Read the nearby Jewish explanation: Genesis 32:2

Passage or chapter context. Read the contextual study.

Masoretic Text Hebrew–English

32:1 [MT 32:2] Jacob went on his way, and the angels of God met him.

Septuagint Greek–English

Greek adds Jacob looking up and seeing God’s encamped host before the angelic encounter. Common English 32:1 corresponds to 32:2 in both the Hebrew source and Rahlfs–Hanhart. Sources: BHS, Genesis 32:2; Rahlfs–Hanhart, Genesis 32:2.

Passage or chapter context. Read the contextual study.

32:10  Disparate

Masoretic Text Hebrew–English

32:10 [MT 32:11] “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.”

Septuagint Greek–English

32:10 [RH 32:11] “All the righteousness and truth You have shown Your servant suffice for me. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.”

1. Direct word comparison and meaning

Hebrew expresses Jacob’s unworthiness of the kindness and faithfulness he has received; Greek describes their sufficiency for him. This changes the force of his acknowledgment within the prayer. The difficult Greek present expression is preserved without changing it into a command. Sources: BHS, Genesis 32:11; Rahlfs–Hanhart, Genesis 32:11.

Compare the English wording

Highlighted words differ in these English renderings. Punctuation and capitalization are ignored. An unmatched English word does not by itself prove a Hebrew or Greek omission.

Masoretic Text Hebrew–English[MT 32:11] “I am unworthy of all the kindness and faithfulness You have shown Your servant. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.”
Septuagint Greek–English[RH 32:11] “All the righteousness and truth You have shown Your servant suffice for me. With my staff I crossed this Jordan, and now I have become two camps.”

2. Rabbinic/Jewish explanation, teaching, and understanding

Comment on this verse. Rashi on Genesis 32:11:1 explains: קטנתי מכל החסדים I AM TOO UNWORTHY OF ALL THE MERCIES (This may be rendered “I am small — unworthy — because of all the kindnesses) — My merits are diminished in consequence of all the kindness and truth which You have already shown me. For this reason I am afraid: perhaps, since You made these promises to me, I have become depraved (נתקלקלתי) by sin (another version of Rashi has נתלכלכתי, I have become defiled by sin) and this may cause me to be delivered unto Esau’s power (Shabbat 32a).

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Prophetic and patristic reception. Hosea 12:3–5 recalls Jacob’s struggle, tears, and plea for favor. St Augustine, City of God XVI.39 gives a Christian typological reading of the wrestling and blessing. Such interpretation is distinct from the anatomical comparison and should not be used to turn the injury description into a modern diagnosis.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

Text: Disparate. Read this textual assessment with the reception comparison below.

Jacob's prayer acknowledges dependence on divine help in both versions. Rabbinic exposition and Christian reflection on grace illuminate that dependence. Unworthiness and sufficiency express related but different aspects of gratitude, and their theological compatibility does not remove the textual distinction.

5. How and why the differences arose

Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. The Hebrew idiom of smallness or unworthiness can be recast through the sufficiency of divine kindness. This may reflect interpretation of an expression of humility. The Greek's difficult present construction should remain unresolved rather than be replaced with a smoother but unsupported request.

32:25  Disparate

Masoretic Text Hebrew–English

32:25 [MT 32:26] When the man saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched Jacob’s hip socket, and Jacob’s hip was dislocated as he wrestled with him.

Septuagint Greek–English

32:25 [RH 32:26] And when the man saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the broad part of his thigh; and the broad part of Jacob’s thigh became numb in his wrestling with him.

1. Direct word comparison and meaning

Hebrew describes a dislocated hip socket; Greek describes numbness in the broad part of the thigh. The reported bodily outcome changes substantially. The note identifies the textual descriptions without imposing a modern diagnosis. Sources: BHS, Genesis 32:26; Rahlfs–Hanhart, Genesis 32:26.

Compare the English wording

Highlighted words differ in these English renderings. Punctuation and capitalization are ignored. An unmatched English word does not by itself prove a Hebrew or Greek omission.

Masoretic Text Hebrew–English[MT 32:26] When the man saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched Jacob’s hip socket, and Jacob’s hip was dislocated as he wrestled with him.
Septuagint Greek–English[RH 32:26] And when the man saw that he could not prevail against him, he touched the broad part of his thigh; and the broad part of Jacob’s thigh became numb in his wrestling with him.

2. Rabbinic/Jewish explanation, teaching, and understanding

Comment on this verse. Rashi on Genesis 32:26:1 explains: ויגע בכף ירכו HE TOUCHED THE HOLLOW OF HIS THIGH — The upper thigh-bone that is sunk in the hip is called כף because the flesh on it (on this bone) has the form of the hollow part of a pot-ladle (כף).

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Prophetic and patristic reception. Hosea 12:3–5 recalls Jacob’s struggle, tears, and plea for favor. St Augustine, City of God XVI.39 gives a Christian typological reading of the wrestling and blessing. Such interpretation is distinct from the anatomical comparison and should not be used to turn the injury description into a modern diagnosis.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

Text: Disparate. Read this textual assessment with the reception comparison below.

The injury marks the encounter and grounds a later food practice. Rabbinic law develops that bodily detail, while Hosea and Christian reception emphasize struggle, blessing, and dependence. Those interpretations should not make dislocation and numbness anatomically identical or claim greater medical precision than the texts provide.

5. How and why the differences arose

Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. An unfamiliar anatomical term and a verb describing injury may have received different lexical interpretations. The Greek stresses a numbed condition where Hebrew describes displacement. Ancient vocabulary and differing bodily description provide plausible explanations without requiring a modern diagnosis or evidence of negligent copying.

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Prophetic and patristic reception. Hosea 12:3–5 recalls Jacob’s struggle, tears, and plea for favor. St Augustine, City of God XVI.39 gives a Christian typological reading of the wrestling and blessing. Such interpretation is distinct from the anatomical comparison and should not be used to turn the injury description into a modern diagnosis.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

Text: Disparate. Read this textual assessment with the reception comparison below.

Rashi connects the new name with acknowledged entitlement to blessing, while Christian interpretation often reads the encounter through struggle and divine condescension. The name's etymological explanation remains distinct in each column. A theological synthesis should preserve that linguistic difficulty rather than remove it.

5. How and why the differences arose

Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. The explanation of Israel's name depends on Hebrew wordplay that cannot be reproduced directly in Greek. Interpreting its force through strength and contest can generate a different construction. The verbless ending also requires restraint: supplying a future promise is an editorial choice, not a recovered verb.

1. Direct word comparison and meaning

The dietary explanation recalls distinct injury descriptions: Hebrew’s hip socket and difficult sinew term, and Greek’s numb sinew at the broad part of the thigh. The bodily detail underlying the practice changes. Exact modern anatomical identification remains open. Sources: BHS, Genesis 32:33; Rahlfs–Hanhart, Genesis 32:33.

Septuagint Greek–English[RH 32:33] Therefore the Israelites do not eat the sinew that became numb, which is at the broad part of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the broad part of Jacob’s thigh, the sinew, and it became numb.

2. Rabbinic/Jewish explanation, teaching, and understanding

Comment on this verse. Rashi on Genesis 32:33:1 explains: גיד הנשה THE SINEW OF THE THIGH-VEIN — Why is its name called גיד הנשה? Because it sprang נשה) and rose from its proper position. The word has the meaning of “springing”. Other examples are: (Jeremiah 51:30) “Their strength sprang away (נשתה)” and (41:51) “for God hath made all my trouble spring away from me נַשַּׁנִי)".

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Prophetic and patristic reception. Hosea 12:3–5 recalls Jacob’s struggle, tears, and plea for favor. St Augustine, City of God XVI.39 gives a Christian typological reading of the wrestling and blessing. Such interpretation is distinct from the anatomical comparison and should not be used to turn the injury description into a modern diagnosis.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

Text: Disparate. Read this textual assessment with the reception comparison below.

The injury marks the encounter and grounds a later food practice. Rabbinic law develops that bodily detail, while Hosea and Christian reception emphasize struggle, blessing, and dependence. Those interpretations should not make dislocation and numbness anatomically identical or claim greater medical precision than the texts provide.

5. How and why the differences arose

Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. An unfamiliar anatomical term and a verb describing injury may have received different lexical interpretations. The Greek stresses a numbed condition where Hebrew describes displacement. Ancient vocabulary and differing bodily description provide plausible explanations without requiring a modern diagnosis or evidence of negligent copying.

32:32 Therefore the Israelites do not eat the sinew at the hip socket to this day, because he touched Jacob’s hip socket at that sinew.

Masoretic verse 32:33

Septuagint Greek–English

32:32 [RH 32:33] Therefore the Israelites do not eat the sinew that became numb, which is at the broad part of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the broad part of Jacob’s thigh, the sinew, and it became numb.

1. Direct word comparison and meaning

The dietary explanation recalls distinct injury descriptions: Hebrew’s hip socket and difficult sinew term, and Greek’s numb sinew at the broad part of the thigh. The bodily detail underlying the practice changes. Exact modern anatomical identification remains open. Sources: BHS, Genesis 32:33; Rahlfs–Hanhart, Genesis 32:33.

Compare the English wording

Highlighted words differ in these English renderings. Punctuation and capitalization are ignored. An unmatched English word does not by itself prove a Hebrew or Greek omission.

Masoretic Text Hebrew–EnglishTherefore the Israelites do not eat the sinew at the hip socket to this day, because he touched Jacob’s hip socket at that sinew.
Septuagint Greek–English[RH 32:33] Therefore the Israelites do not eat the sinew that became numb, which is at the broad part of the thigh, to this day, because he touched the broad part of Jacob’s thigh, the sinew, and it became numb.

2. Rabbinic/Jewish explanation, teaching, and understanding

Comment on this verse. Rashi on Genesis 32:33:1 explains: גיד הנשה THE SINEW OF THE THIGH-VEIN — Why is its name called גיד הנשה? Because it sprang נשה) and rose from its proper position. The word has the meaning of “springing”. Other examples are: (Jeremiah 51:30) “Their strength sprang away (נשתה)” and (41:51) “for God hath made all my trouble spring away from me נַשַּׁנִי)".

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Prophetic and patristic reception. Hosea 12:3–5 recalls Jacob’s struggle, tears, and plea for favor. St Augustine, City of God XVI.39 gives a Christian typological reading of the wrestling and blessing. Such interpretation is distinct from the anatomical comparison and should not be used to turn the injury description into a modern diagnosis.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

Text: Disparate. Read this textual assessment with the reception comparison below.

The injury marks the encounter and grounds a later food practice. Rabbinic law develops that bodily detail, while Hosea and Christian reception emphasize struggle, blessing, and dependence. Those interpretations should not make dislocation and numbness anatomically identical or claim greater medical precision than the texts provide.

5. How and why the differences arose

Proposed explanation; origin unresolved. An unfamiliar anatomical term and a verb describing injury may have received different lexical interpretations. The Greek stresses a numbed condition where Hebrew describes displacement. Ancient vocabulary and differing bodily description provide plausible explanations without requiring a modern diagnosis or evidence of negligent copying.

Masoretic Text Hebrew–English

8:26 (H 8:22) Moses said, “It would not be right to do so, for we would sacrifice to YHWH our God what is an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice what is an abomination to them before their eyes, will they not stone us?

Septuagint Greek–English

8:22 Moses said, “This cannot be done, for we would sacrifice to the Lord our God what the Egyptians regard as abominations. If we sacrifice these before their eyes, we shall be stoned.

1. Direct word comparison and meaning

Greek makes the stoning an assertion; Hebrew asks a rhetorical question [G8]. The precise reason for Egyptian abhorrence is not supplied in this verse.

Textual sources. BHS, Exodus 8 · Rahlfs–Hanhart (2006), Exodus 8. See the independent verse references in the two readings.

Reference crosswalk. Earlier navigation: 8:26 → RH 8:22.

Compare the English wording

Highlighted words differ in these English renderings. Punctuation and capitalization are ignored. An unmatched English word does not by itself prove a Hebrew or Greek omission.

Masoretic Text Hebrew–EnglishMoses said, “It would not be right to do so, for we would sacrifice to YHWH our God what is an abomination to the Egyptians. If we sacrifice what is an abomination to them before their eyes, will they not stone us?
Septuagint Greek–EnglishMoses said, “This cannot be done, for we would sacrifice to the Lord our God what the Egyptians regard as abominations. If we sacrifice these before their eyes, we shall be stoned.

2. Rabbinic/Jewish explanation, teaching, and understanding

Comment on the corresponding Hebrew verse.

Rashi on Exodus 8:22:1 — source excerpt

תועבת מצרים THE ABOMINATION OF THE EGYPTIANS — This means: that which the Egyptians reverence (their idol), just as, (2 Kings 23:13) “and for Milcom the abomination (תועבת) of the children of Ammon”, but in relation to the Israelites it (Scripture) calls it תועבה. We may explain these words in another sense also: תועבת מצרים — The act of sacrifice which we practise is a hateful thing to the Egyptians seing that we sacrifice their god (sheep which were reverenced as gods in Egypt).

The first available comment is reproduced in full; other comments on the verse may discuss additional readings. This is attributed exegesis, not added wording in either biblical column.

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Passage or chapter context. Read the contextual study.

Acts 7:35–36 remembers Moses as deliverer and worker of signs. Romans 9:17–18 cites the declaration to Pharaoh in Exodus 9:16 while discussing mercy and hardening. The citation is specific; the other plague details supply narrative context.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

Text: Similar; contextual reception: Unclassified — different scope. The source comparison states what each cited interpreter explains and why the applications differ. This contextual profile does not claim a verse-specific contradiction or change the textual badge.

Contextual reception. Paul’s argument concerns divine action in the history of salvation. Rashi’s verse comments distinguish speakers, actions, and the course of the plagues. The shared story permits comparison, but neither a different detail nor a different argumentative purpose establishes wholesale doctrinal opposition.

חמשה בקר וגו׳ [HE SHALL PAY] FIVE OF THE HERD etc. — Rabban Jochanan ben Zaccai said, “The Omnipresent has much consideration for the honour of His creatures: when an ox — an animal that can walk by itself — has been stolen and sold or slaughtered, in which case the thief had not to degrade himself by carrying it on his shoulder, he has to pay fivefold restitution. Rabbi Meir said, “Come and see how great is the virtue of labour: In the case of the theft of an ox which he (the thief) withdrew from its labour, thereby causing a loss to its owner, he has to repay five oxen, in the case of a lamb which he has not withdrawn from its labour — only four (Bava Kamma 79b).

3. Saints/Christian explanation, teaching, and understanding

Matthew 5:38–42 develops a teaching about nonretaliation from the retaliation formula. This is a broader ethical connection, not direct commentary on the difficult Greek death-in-return clause.

4. Combined classification: Text, Rabbis, and Medieval Saints

MT/LXX: Disparate; Rabbinic/Christian: Unclassified — different scope. Rashi distinguishes the thief's repayment from the householder's liability for unjustified killing. Christian teaching against retaliation is a broader ethical comparison. The Greek death-in-return clause requires its own grammatical examination; it cannot be harmonized simply by importing the Hebrew restitution clause.

Text: Proposed explanation; historical origin unresolved. The compressed legal sequence permits difficult pronoun and clause attachments. Greek may reflect a different formulation of liability or a different interpretation of the transition into restitution. The present comparison cannot establish which explanation is preferable, and should not manufacture a smooth reconstructed original. Reception: Rashi explains liability and restitution; Matthew’s broader ethical teaching does not parse the difficult Greek clause. 2. Rabbinic/Jewish explanation, teaching, and understanding

Comment on the corresponding Hebrew verse.

Rashi on Exodus 22:19:1 — source excerpt

לָאֱלֹהִים means TO IDOLS — If the word (a noun) were punctuated לֵאלֹהִים, with Tzéré under the first ל it would be necessary to define it more closely by adding the adjective אחרים = strange (gods — idols); now, however, that it says לָאֱלֹהִים it is not necessary to define it more closely by adding the word אחרים. For wherever ל or ב are prefixed to a word if it (the prefix) be punctuated with Chataph (שוא), as e. g., לְמֶלֶךְ a king, לְמִדְבָּר, to a desert, לָעִיר, to a city, it must be explained to which king, to which desert, to which city. The same is the case if the ל or ב has a Chirik instead of a Sheva which happens when they are placed before a word beginning with Sheva, as e .g., in לִמְלָכִים for kings, לִרְגָלִים, for festivals, (quoted from Mishnah Rosh Hashanah 1:1) it is necessary to state for which kings or festivals, and if he does not state this, all kings and festivals are implied by these words. Similarly here: the word לַאלֹהִים “to gods”, would imply “all gods”, including even Him of Whom the term אלהים is used in a holy sense (i. e. the Most High God). When, however, it (the prefix) is vowelled with Patach (or Kametz if the following letter cannot take Dagesh), as לַמֶּלֶךְ and לַמִּדְבָּר and לָעִיר it is quite plain which king one is speaking of, and similarly in the case of לָעִיר “to the city”, it is quite plain of which city one is speaking. In the same way, לָאֱלֹהִים, to the gods, means to those gods which in another passage you have been forbidden to worship. A similar instance is, (Psalms 86:8) אין כמוך בָאֱלֹהִים, “there is none like unto Thee among the gods” — because he did not more closely define it by the addition of some word like אחרים, it was necessary for him to vowel the ל with Patach (Kametz).
